Judgment

1. The appellant is aggrieved by the impugned judgment dated 10/09/2018 of Ld. MM-06,
South-East District, Saket Court, vide which he was convicted for offence U/s. 279/304A IPC &
Section 3/181 M.V. Act.

Vide order on sentence dated 20/09/2018, he was sentenced to undergo Simple Imprisonment for a period of one month for offence U/s. 279 IPC and sentenced to undergo Rigorous Imprisonment of two years for offence U/s. 304A IPC.
He was sentenced to undergo Simple Imprisonment for one month for offence U/s. 3/181 M.V. Act, in case FIR No. 49/2017, PS Kalkaji.

In addition, appellant was directed to pay a sum of Rs.20,000/- to legal heirs of deceased,
as compensation, in default of which, he was ordered to undergo Simple Imprisonment of 07 days.
All the sentences were directed to run concurrently.

2. The prosecution case in brief is that on 01/02/2017, at about 09:00 AM, near Jhuggi No.
S-04/119, Sarvodaya Camp, Sudarshan Mujal Marg, New Delhi, within the jurisdiction of PS Kalkaji,

sentences.text: The FIR was registered on complaint of eye-witness/complainant Amar Chand, son of the deceased/victim.

On the basis of reply of owner of offending vehicle in pursuance of notice U/s. 133 M.V. Act, accused Pawan Kumar was arrested on 04/02/2017 and, after completion of investigation, charge-sheet was filed for the offence U/s.
279/304A IPC & Section 3/181 M.V. Act.
Charge for offence U/s. 279/304A IPC & Section 3/181 M.V. Act was framed against the accused, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.

3. As per Trial Court record, to prove its case, the prosecution examined following 05 witnesses during trial of the case:
(i) PW1/complainant Amar Chand, eye-witness to the incident, deposed that there was a shop of tyre puncture of one Raju, outside his Jhuggi No. S-04/119, Sarvodya Camp, Kalkaji.
He deposed that on 01/02/2017 when he was standing outside his jhuggi, Raju was repairing puncture on tyre of a Taxi bearing No. HR-69C-5592.

He deposed that at about 09:00AM his mother i.e. deceased Harnandi came out of the jhuggi and when she was picking garbage, the driver of aforementioned taxi, while driving it in a rash and negligent manner, hit his mother and she became unconscious.
He deposed that he apprehended the taxi driver at the spot, who disclosed his name as Pawan.
Thereafter, he took his mother in the offending taxi to Safdarjung Hospital, where the doctor declared her as brought dead.
He deposed that the accused ran away after leaving the offending taxi in hospital.
In the meantime, police officials reached the hospital, recorded his statement Ex. PW1/A and seized the offending car vide memo Ex. PW1/B.
He deposed that he again went to the spot on the same day and IO prepared site plan Ex. PW1/C at this instance.
After postmortem, he received the body of his mother on 02/02/2017 at AIIMS Hospital, through identification statement Ex. PW1/D.

He deposed that on 04/02/2017 when he went to police station to enquire about progress of the case, he saw accused Pawan there and immediately identified him,
and police arrested him in his presence vide arrest memo Ex. PW1/E.
He identified accused Pawan in Court.
He also identified five photographs Ex. P-1 (Colly.) of the alleged offending car.

(ii) PW2 Ct. Baldev deposed about joining of investigation alongwith IO on 01/02/2017, collecting of MLC of deceased Harnandi by IO as well as recording of statement of eye witness Amar Chand at Safdarjung Hospital, preparation of rukka, shifting of deceased to AIIMS Mortuary for postmortem,
handing over of body to its relatives after postmortem and seizure of offending vehicle i.e. Taxi.
(iii) PW3 Ct. Pankaj deposed about joining of investigation alongwith IO on 04/02/2017, seizure of RC of offending vehicle No. HR-69C-5592 vide memo Ex. PW3/A alongwith its insurance vide memo Ex. PW3/C, DL of accused driver vide memo Ex. PW3/B, preparation of arrest as well as personal search memo of accused.

Since the accused, through his separate statements recorded U/s. 294 CrPC, on 05/07/2018 and 23/07/2018, admitted contents and genuineness of the documents i.e. (i) registration of FIR, MLC No.5526, PM Report No. 158/2017, documents related to RC, RTO, Sonipat, DL, RTO, Assand and Insurance Bharti Axa General Insurance, all Ex. P-1 to Ex. P-6, respectively and (ii) Mechanical Inspection Report dated 02/02/2017, Ex. P-7, the requirement to prove the said documents through concerned PWs was obviated.
5. Statement of accused Pawan Kumar was recorded U/s. 313 CrPC.
He denied all incriminating evidence and asserted that he was falsely implicated in the case.
He stated that he did not visit Raju puncture wala on the day of incident and helped the complainant on humanitarian ground to take his mother to hospital.
He stated that the complainant in connivance with the IO, falsely implicated him in this case to obtain claim under relevant provision of M.V. Act.
He did not examine any witness in his defence.

6. Upon hearing the final arguments from both sides, Ld. Trial Court vide its judgment dated 10/09/2018 held the appellant/accused guilty of offence U/s. 279/304A IPC & Section 3/181 M.V.
Act and sentenced him vide order on sentence dated 20/09/2018.
7.
Ld. Counsel for appellant argued that Ld. Trial Court did not properly appreciate the evidence and wrongly convicted the appellant.
It was argued that the impugned judgment was completely against the weight of evidence; the evidence did not indicate towards culpability of the appellant.
The appellant prayed for setting aside of his conviction and for acquittal of the offence U/s. 279/304A IPC & Section 3/181 M.V. Act.

sentences.text: Ld. Addl. PP for State/respondent has opposed the appeal stating that prosecution proved its case against the appellant and Ld. Trial Court rightly convicted and sentenced him.
9. I have heard rival contentions from both sides and perused the record.

Deposition of eye-witness PW1 Amar Chand:-
10.
PW1/complainant Amar Chand, eye-witness to the incident, deposed that there was a tyre puncture shop of one Raju, near his Jhuggi No. S-04/119, Sarvodya Camp, Kalkaji.
He deposed that on 01/02/2017 when he was standing outside his jhuggi, Raju was repairing puncture on tyre of a Taxi bearing No. HR-69C-5592.

He deposed that at about 09:00AM his mother i.e. deceased Harnandi came out of the jhuggi and when she was picking garbage, the driver of aforementioned taxi, while driving it in a rash and negligent manner, hit his mother and she became unconscious.
He deposed that he apprehended the taxi driver i.e. accused Pawan at the spot.
In cross-examination, PW1 explained that the taxi of accused Pawan was standing in front of shop of Raju and was facing towards jhuggi of PW1.
PW1 admitted that when the car started it ran towards the direction that it was facing.
He admitted that his mother was picking garbage from in front of her jhuggi at the time of incident.
The road in front of his jhuggi was about 60- 70 feet wide and was not very crowded at the time of incident.
It is observed that in the cross-examination, accused/appellant Pawan Kumar himself confirmed facts of the incident by putting incriminating suggestions to PW1.

The suggestions made to prosecution witness by the defence counsel and reply to such suggestions form part of the evidence and can be relied upon by the Court alongwith other evidence on record to determine the guilt of the accused [Ref. Balu Sudam Khalde & Anr. Vs. State of Maharashtra (2023) SCC Online SC 355].
Corroboration of testimony of PW1 by Mechanical Inspection Report of the Car :-
11.

It is observed that the accused admitted mechanical inspection report Ex. P-7 in his statement U/s.
294 CrPC.
As per report, as a fresh damage, left front door outside handle of the car was found broken.
The testimony of PW1 stood corroborated in this regard by mechanical inspection report of the offending car.

Medical Evidence :-
12.
As per postmortem report Ex. P-3, deceased Harnandi sustained multiple head and chest injuries as well as laceration on the lungs.
She expired by shock due to polytrauma caused by blunt external force which could be possible in the alleged case of road traffic accident.

Counsel for appellant argued that the appellant had sufficiently explained in statement recorded U/s. 313 CrPC that PW1 falsely implicated him just to obtain false claim under M.V. Act from MACT Court, although, the appellant had not caused the accident and rather helped the complainant on humanitarian ground to rush his mother to hospital.
In this regard, it is observed that PW1 was not known to the appellant before the incident, leave alone the question of enmity between them.
PW1 had no motive to falsely implicate the appellant if he had not caused the accident.
The appellant failed to show that PW1 was somehow interested in getting him convicted for some extraneous reason [Ref. Amit Vs. State of U.P. (2012) 4 SCC 107].

sentences.text: Counsel for appellant argued that even if it is accepted that appellant was getting his punctured car repaired beside the jhuggi of PW1, his car could not have picked up enough speed at such a short distance to crush deceased Harnandi in the accident.
It is observed that such a plea is completely absurd and untenable; a stationary car can pick-up enough speed within short distance to seriously injure a pedestrian in a head-on impact.
15. The testimonies of all prosecution witnesses are consistent and corroborative to each other.
The prosecution brought home the charged offence against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt.

16. Hon'ble Supreme Court has held in Ravi Kapur Vs. State of Rajasthan (2012) 9 SCC 284 that - 12.Rash and negligent driving has to be examined in the light of facts and circumstances of a given case.

entities.text: Ravi Kapur Vs. State of Rajasthan (2012) 9 SCC 284
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is a fact incapable of being construed or seen in isolation.
It must be examined in the light of attended circumstances.
A person who drives a vehicle on the road is liable to be held responsible for the act as well as for the result.
It may not be always possible to determine with reference to the speed of a vehicle whether a person was driving rashly and negligently.
Both these acts presuppose an abnormal conduct.
Even when one is driving a vehicle at a slow speed but recklessly and negligently, it would amount to "rash and negligent driving" within the meaning of language of Section 279 IPC.
That is why the Legislature in its wisdom has used the words "manner so rash or negligent as to endanger human life".

The preliminary condition, thus, are that - (a) it is the manner in which the vehicle is driven; (b) it be driven either rashly or negligently; and (c) such rash or negligent driving should be such as to endanger human life.
Once these ingredients are satisfied, the penalty contemplated under Section 279 IPC is attracted.

13.'Negligence' means omission to do something which a reasonable and prudent person guided by the considerations which ordinary regulate human affairs would do or doing something which a prudent and reasonable person guided by similar considerations would not do.
Negligence is not an absolute term but is a relative one; it is rather a comparative term.
It is difficult to state with precision any mathematically exact formula by which negligence or lack of it can be infallibly measured in a given case.

Whether there exists negligence per se or the course of conduct amounts to negligence will normally depend upon the attending and surrounding facts and circumstances which have to be taken into consideration by the Court.

In a given case, even not doing what one was Pawan Kumar vs State Of Nct Of Delhi on 15 December, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/174720496/
5 ought to do can constitute negligence.

sentences.text: 14.The Court has to adopt another parameter i.e. 'reasonable care' in determining the question of negligence or contributory negligence.

The doctrine of reasonable care imposes an obligation or a duty upon a person (for example a driver) to care for the pedestrian on the road and this duty attains a higher degree when the pedestrians happen to be children of tender years.

It is axiomatic to say that while driving a vehicle on a public way, there is an implicit duty cast on the drivers to see that their driving does not endanger the life of the right users of the road, may be either vehicular users or pedestrians.
They are expected to take sufficient care to avoid danger to others.
15.The other principle that is pressed in aid by the courts in such cases is the doctrine of res ipsa loquitur.

This doctrine serves two purposes - one that an accident may by its nature be more consistent with its being caused by negligence for which the opposite party is responsible than by any other causes and that in such a case, the mere fact of the accident is prima facie evidence of such negligence.
Secondly, it is to avoid hardship in cases where the claimant is able to prove the accident but cannot prove how the accident occurred.
The courts have also applied the principle of res ipsa loquitur in cases where no direct evidence was brought on record.
The Act itself contains a provision which concerns with the consequences of driving vehicle dangerously alike the provision in the IPC that the vehicle is driven in a manner dangerous to public life.
Where a person does such an offence he is punished as per the provisions of Section 184 of the Act.
The courts have also taken the concept of 'culpable rashness' and 'culpable negligence' into consideration in cases of road accidents.

'Culpable rashness' is acting with the consciousness that mischievous and illegal consequences may follow but with the hope that they will not and often with the belief that the actor has taken sufficient precautions to prevent their happening.
The imputability arises from acting despite consciousness (luxuria).

'Culpable negligence' is acting without the consciousness that the illegal and mischievous effect will follow, but in circumstances which show that the actor has not exercised the caution incumbent upon him and that if he had, he would have had the consciousness.
The imputability arises from the neglect of civic duty of circumspection.
In such a case the mere fact of accident is prima facie evidence of such negligence.

This maxim suggests that on the circumstances of a given case the res speaks and is eloquent because the facts stand unexplained, with the result that the natural and reasonable inference from the facts, not a conjectural inference, shows that the act is attributable to some person's negligent conduct.
[Ref. Justice Rajesh Tandon's 'An Exhaustive Commentary on Motor Vehicles Act, 1988' (1st Edn., 2010].
17. The accident occurred at 09:00AM, during day time.

The appellant drove the taxi car from stationary position without taking reasonable care to avoid accident with the victim lady, who was clearing the garbage in front of her jhuggi, on side of the road.

Appellant did not have licence to drive a commercial vehicle, for which he was rightly convicted for offence U/s. 3/181 M.V. Act.
18.
The impugned judgment dated 10/09/2018 is reasonable and is based on correct appreciation of facts and evidence.
The appellant was rightly convicted for offence U/s. 279/304A IPC & Section 3/181 M.V. Act.

There is no substance in appeal and, so far as it impugns the judgment of conviction,
it stands dismissed.
The issue of sentence shall be considered on completion of due procedure.
